questions.question: Is your system an AI system within the meaning of the AI Act?
questions.ownerContext: An AI system is usually software, or a component of software, that infers (derives) how to produce an output or course of action from patterns learned from data (machine learning) or by reasoning over logic (logic-based) or knowledge (knowledge-based), rather than merely following precise, pre-set instructions. It can operate with varying degrees of autonomy; it does not have to function entirely without human involvement. While not required, it can keep learning and change its behaviour while in use.​‌

questions.question: Is the AI System or its output used exclusively for one or more of the following matters?
questions.ownerContext:
MILITARY, DEFENCE AND NATIONAL SECURITY
The AI Act does not cover an AI system that is used only for military, defence or national security purposes. It does not matter who uses it: a public body and a private company are treated alike. If the same system is also used for any other purpose, for example civilian, humanitarian or law enforcement, even occasionally, the exclusion is lost.

SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
The AI Act also does not cover AI systems that are developed and used only for scientific research and development. This includes research in all fields, not only technical sciences, but also the humanities and social sciences.

KEY CONDITION: "EXCLUSIVELY"
The key word is "exclusively". If the system is also used for any other purpose (for example civilian, commercial or law enforcement), the AI Act applies. The same is true if a system first built for military use is later used, even temporarily, for civilian or humanitarian purposes.

questions.question: Is the AI System used by a public authority of a third country OR an international organisation for international cooperation or law enforcement?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not apply to public authorities of non-EU countries or to international organisations when they use AI systems as part of cooperation with the EU or with EU Member States in the fight against crime or in judicial matters.

CONDITIONS (ALL MUST BE MET)
All of the following conditions must be met:
- the user is a public authority of a non-EU country or an international organisation,
- the system is used under an international cooperation framework or agreement on law enforcement or judicial cooperation with the EU or with one or more Member States,
- the non-EU country or organisation provides adequate safeguards to protect people's fundamental rights and freedoms.

RESPONSIBILITY OF EU AND NATIONAL AUTHORITIES
EU and national authorities that use the results of such systems in the EU still remain responsible for complying with EU law.

REFERENCES

questions.question: Is the AI system used in research, testing or development activity and has not been placed on the market or put into service?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not apply to research, testing and development of AI systems or models before they are offered on the market or put into use. This also covers product-oriented, commercial work, such as a company developing its own AI product.

END OF THE EXCLUSION
The exclusion ends when the system is placed on the market or put into service. From that moment, the AI Act applies.

TESTING IN REAL-WORLD CONDITIONS
Testing in real-world conditions (outside the lab, with real users or real situations) is not excluded and is regulated by the AI Act.

OTHER APPLICABLE EU LAW
Even when the exclusion applies, the work must still comply with other EU law, such as data protection rules, research ethics rules and sector-specific rules.

questions.question: Does a natural person use the system exclusively in the course of a personal, non-professional activity?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not impose obligations on individuals who use AI systems only for purely private purposes, for example at home, for hobbies or in family life. Such use is considered lower risk than professional or business use.

WHEN THE EXCLUSION DOES NOT APPLY
The exclusion does not apply when the system is used:
- for work, business or other professional activity,
- in an organised social or non-profit activity, for example in an association or foundation,
- for both private and professional purposes (mixed use).

INCOME FROM THE ACTIVITY
Earning some income does not automatically exclude private use, as long as the activity is not carried out professionally, as a business or as another organised activity.

SCOPE OF THE EXCLUSION AND CIVIL LIABILITY
This exclusion concerns only the private user. It does not release the provider of the system from its obligations. The private user may still be liable under civil law for damage caused intentionally or through gross negligence.

questions.question: Is the system made available under a free and open-source licence?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE AND CONDITIONS
The AI Act generally does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences. To benefit from this exclusion, the system must meet all of the following conditions:
- Publicly available: anyone can access it on equal terms. Only basic steps, such as accepting terms of use, downloading the system or creating a user account, are acceptable.
- Free: there is no monetisation. Monetisation includes charging a price, charging for technical support or related services (also through software platforms), or using personal data for purposes other than improving security, compatibility or interoperability. Sharing the system in an open repository is not monetisation. Transactions between micro-enterprises are also not treated as monetisation.
- Open: key technical information, such as model weights, architecture and information on use, is publicly available, and the licence allows users not only to use, but also to modify and distribute the system.

LIMITS OF THE EXCLUSION
The exclusion does not apply if the system is placed on the market or put into service as a high-risk AI system, as a prohibited AI practice, or as a system subject to transparency obligations (for example, a system that generates or manipulates images, sound or video, such as deepfakes).

questions.question: System type and components: What kind of AI or automated decision-making is involved (e.g. large language model, classical ML classifier, computer vision model, rules engine, scoring algorithm, or a combination)? What are the specific models or components used, including names, versions, and providers where applicable?
System position: Is the AI the product itself, a component embedded in a wider product, or an API consumed by third parties?
Architecture: What are the main components and their boundaries? Which parts are AI-driven and which are deterministic? What are the key runtime dependencies?

Data flows: What types of data does the system take as input, where does it come from, and does it include sensitive or regulated categories? Does the output directly trigger a downstream action, or does it require human approval before anything happens?
Affected population: Who or what does the system’s output affect: the end user, a third party, or a downstream automated system?
Oversight and auditability: Is a human in, on, or in command of the loop? Are inputs, outputs, and decisions logged, and if so, for how long and retrievable by whom?
Update cadence: How often are models or decision logic updated or retrained, and who controls that process?
Failure behaviour: What does the system do when it cannot produce a reliable output or encounters an error?
What is the current development stage (e.g. proof of concept, pilot, beta, production)?
What is the planned rollout timeline and target regions or user groups?
Has any deployment already occurred, and if so, at what scale?
What is the AI system intended to be used for and what use cases does this AI system have specifically within the organisation?
questions.ownerContext:
The ‘intended purpose’ means the use for which an AI system is intended by the provider, including the specific context and conditions of use, [as specified in the information supplied by the provider in the instructions for use, promotional or sales materials and statements, as well as in the technical documentation] (Art. 3(12) EU AI Act).

When describing the intended purpose, it should be clearly stated:

- which business or operational tasks the AI system is intended to perform or support,
- which outputs the system provides (e.g., classifications, recommendations, or predictions),
- for what purpose these outputs are used (e.g., process acceleration, quality improvement, or decision support).

All intended purposes must be listed completely.

If a system has multiple use cases or applications, all of them must be identified, as the intended purpose is a key factor in determining the AI system's risk classification.

Does the AI system use biometric categorisation systems that categorise individual persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
Art. 5(1)(g) prohibits biometric categorisation systems that categorise natural persons individually on the basis of their biometric data in order to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Such categorisation systems are prohibited under the EU AI Act.

KEY TERMS
"Biometric data" means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data (Art. 3(34)).
A "biometric categorisation system" assigns natural persons to specific categories on the basis of their biometric data (Art. 3(40)); the definition does not cover a feature that is purely ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons (for example, filters on online marketplaces that let customers preview a product on themselves; Recital (16).

INDIVIDUAL CATEGORISATION
The prohibition applies only where persons are categorised individually. Systems that categorise a whole group without looking at the individual, or that are aimed at broad groups, are outside the prohibition (Commission Guidelines; commentary).

EXCLUSIONS
The prohibition does not cover the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets (for example, to make training data representative of all demographic groups) or the categorisation of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. The commentary notes that the wording of this exclusion is not fully clear.

REFERENCES
E.J. Kindt, C. Jasserand, commentary on Art. 5 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024

questions.question: Does the system use subliminal, intentionally manipulative, or deceptive techniques?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness, or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, so that they take a decision they would not otherwise have taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Refers to subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that impair informed decision-making and cause or are reasonably likely to cause harm.

THREE TYPES OF TECHNIQUE
Subliminal techniques act below the threshold of awareness. Purposefully manipulative techniques need not be subliminal; they rest on not disclosing the real intent to influence thoughts, emotions or decisions to a predefined effect. Deceptive techniques build a false picture of the world through deliberately misleading information.

EFFECT ON BEHAVIOUR AND HARM
The technique alone is not enough: the objective or effect must be a material change of behaviour through a significant impairment of informed decision-making. Harm may be psychological, physical, economic or social, and may affect the person concerned or others exposed to that person's conduct. 

LIMITS
According to the Commission Guidelines, intent is sufficient but not necessary, and a plausible causal link between the technique, the distortion of behaviour and the harm is always required. Lawful persuasion, legitimate commercial practices such as advertising and lawful medical treatment fall outside the prohibition.

REFERENCES
E.J. Kindt, C. Jasserand, commentary on Art. 5 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024

questions.question: Could the use of the AI system exploit a vulnerability of a person or a particular group of persons  due to age, disability, or particular social or economic situations with the aim or effect of manipulating their behaviour in a way that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that exploits vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or the effect of materially distorting their behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm.

VULNERABLE GROUPS
"Vulnerability" may be due, for example, to age, disability or a particular social or economic situation. Age covers children and older persons; disability covers any cause or degree; the commentary gives people in a homelessness crisis and indebted people as examples of persons who are particularly sensitive owing to their socio-economic situation.

LIMITS
According to the Commission Guidelines, a system is not automatically caught because it is inadvertently biased or not designed in an accessible manner; the prohibition requires that the system exploits the vulnerability, for example by targeting vulnerable groups.

REFERENCES

questions.question: Does the AI system evaluate or classify any person over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics (known, inferred or predicted), and does this result in either or both of (a) detrimental or unfavourable treatment of any person in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected; or (b) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the person's social behaviour or its gravity?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
Art. 5(1)(c) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment (i) in social contexts unrelated to those in which the data was originally generated or collected, or (ii) that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity.

EVALUATION OR CLASSIFICATION
Scoring covers evaluating persons (including assigning a numerical value) and classifying them (including comparing persons by previously assigned values). The evaluation must refer to past, observable behaviour or to personal or personality characteristics that are known, inferred or predicted. The score may be a number, a ranking or a label, the evaluation must rest on data covering a certain period of time (not a one-time rating from a very specific context), and in principle only natural persons and groups of natural persons are covered, not legal entities.

HARMFUL OR UNFAVOURABLE TREATMENT
Harmful treatment means actual damage, while unfavourable treatment means treatment less favourable than that of others even without concrete harm.

questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
This question asks whether law enforcement, or a private party acting on its behalf and under its instructions, uses live biometric identification in places the public can enter, comparing people with a reference database without significant delay. Matching on recorded footage afterwards, one-to-one checks such as unlocking a phone or a passport e-gate, and online spaces, prisons, border control or access-controlled workplaces are outside this prohibition.

THE EXCEPTIONS
Such live use is prohibited by default and possible only where national law permits it and only for three listed purposes: the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons; preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or safety or a genuine terrorist threat; and locating or identifying a suspect of a serious listed offence. Any other purpose, including ordinary crime fighting, stays prohibited.

questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
This question is about AI that predicts whether a particular person will commit a crime. The key word is "solely": the ban applies when the prediction rests only on a profile of the person or on their personality traits and characteristics, for example nationality, place of residence, number of children, level of debt or type of car. It does not apply when the system only supports a human assessment that is already based on objective, verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity, for example where there is already a reasonable suspicion.

EXCEPTION
Predictions about places rather than persons, risk analysis that is not about individuals (for example suspicious transactions of companies) and ordinary business risk checks not aimed at a specific crime. Private companies are not automatically outside the ban, for example when they act on behalf of law enforcement.

questions.question: Does the AI system create or expand facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
Art. 5(1)(e) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or using AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage.

UNTARGETED SCRAPING
Scraping is an automated process of acquiring data. It is untargeted where it is mass collection not justified by a purpose or a specific context. The sources named in the provision are the internet and CCTV, so websites, social media and (city) video monitoring are covered. The best-known case is Clearview AI, whose practices were sanctioned by several data protection authorities under the GDPR.

LIMITS
Scraping restricted to specific individuals or a pre-defined group is targeted and not covered, whereas step-by-step database building that is functionally untargeted is caught. Not covered: scraping of non-facial biometric data, scraping without AI, databases not used for recognition, generative models creating fictitious persons, and reverse image search.

REFERENCES
E.J. Kindt, C. Jasserand, commentary on Art. 5 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024

questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
This question is about AI that works out how a person feels, for example happy, angry or anxious, from biometric data such as their face, voice, gestures or the way they type, when it is used at work or in education. "Workplace" is wide: any physical or virtual place where people carry out tasks for their employer or organisation, including job candidates. Education covers public and private institutions at every level, including applicants.

EXCEPTION
Not covered: reading emotions from written text, physical states such as pain or fatigue, merely noticing a smile or a raised voice without drawing a conclusion about the emotion, and emotions of customers rather than staff. The only exception is a system intended for medical or safety reasons. It is read narrowly: it means therapeutic use or the protection of life and health, not general wellbeing, stress or productivity monitoring.

questions.question: Does the AI system generate or manipulate realistic intimate or explicit representations of identifiable natural persons in pictures, videos, audio or simuliar content  without the required consent?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
This question is about so-called "nudification" AI: systems that create or alter realistic pictures, videos or audio so that they show the intimate parts of a real, identifiable person, or show that person in sexually explicit activity, without that person's explicit consent. "Realistic" means a credible depiction of the person's face, voice or body; cartoons and physically impossible depictions are out. Editing existing intimate material without showing more (for example a new background) is not "manipulation".

WHO IS CAUGHT (ART. 5(1A))
A provider (the party that builds the system) is caught if such material is the system's intended purpose, or a foreseeable, reproducible result of its design without adequate safeguards. A deployer (the party using the system) is caught only if it uses the system for that purpose. Accidental or lawful use, and uses with explicit consent such as virtual try-on or medical applications, are not covered.

REFERENCES
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI), OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026, Art. 1(7) and recitals (10)-(16).

questions.question: Is the AI system used for the creation/manipulation of material or representations in the sense of the EU law provision in guideline 2011/93/EU?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
This question is about AI that creates or alters material showing children in a sexual way. What counts as such material is defined by an EU directive on combating the sexual abuse of children: material that visually depicts a child, or a person who appears to be a child, in real or simulated sexually explicit conduct; depictions of a child's sexual organs for primarily sexual purposes; realistic images of this kind; and live pornographic performances. Wholly or partially synthetic material counts as well.

EXCEPTION
As for intimate images, a provider is caught if such material is the system's intended purpose, or a foreseeable, reproducible result of its design without adequate safeguards. A deployer is caught only if it uses the system for that purpose. The ban does not apply where a "without right" defence exists under national law, for example authorities producing material for criminal proceedings or legitimate testing.

questions.ownerContext:
HIGH-RISK AI SYSTEM
The question is whether your AI system is itself a product, or is built into a product, that is already regulated by EU product-safety legislation (for example machinery, toys, lifts, radio equipment, medical devices, vehicles or aviation). A 'safety component' is a part whose purpose is to prevent or reduce risks to people's health or safety or to property, or whose failure would endanger them. Features that only optimise performance, efficiency, comfort or quality control are not safety components; being built into a safety-regulated product is not enough.

CONDITIONS
Two conditions must both be met: the system is (or is a safety component of) such a product, and that product must be subject to an assessment by an independent third party under its product legislation. Products that need such an assessment only for other reasons, such as radio interference, do not count.

questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act names eight broad areas where AI can be high-risk: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and training, employment, essential services and benefits, law enforcement, migration and border control, and justice and democratic processes. Being active in one of these areas is only the first filter: only the specific uses listed under each area count, not every system that happens to operate there. 

What matters is the purpose for which your organisation intends the system to be used, as described in its documentation and promotional material. It does not matter whether the system is already running, or whether a human takes the final decision. Where a listed use refers to individuals, a system that only assesses companies is outside, while one that also assesses individuals is inside.

questions.question: Does the AI system use remote biometric identification for any purpose other than to confirm that a particular person is the person he or she claims to be?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS COVERED
Three kinds of systems that rely on biometric data, meaning data derived from a person's face, fingerprints, voice, gait or similar physical or behavioural features.

Remote biometric identification means recognising people without their active involvement, typically at a distance, by comparing their biometric data with a reference database. A one-to-one check whose only purpose is to confirm that someone is who they claim to be (for example unlocking a device or entering premises) is excluded.

Biometric categorisation is relevant only where biometric data is used to infer sensitive characteristics such as ethnic origin, health, religion or political opinions. Emotion recognition means inferring emotions or intentions from biometric data; physical states such as fatigue or pain, and merely detecting an obvious smile or gesture, are not emotion recognition.

questions.question: Will the AI system be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, such as water, gas, heating, electricity, or road traffic?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS COVERED
AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity.

SAFETY COMPONENT 
Safety components of critical infrastructure are systems used to directly protect the physical integrity of critical infrastructure or the health and safety of persons and property, but which are not necessary for the infrastructure to function. Their failure or malfunctioning might directly lead to risks to the physical integrity of the infrastructure and thus to health and safety. Components used solely for cybersecurity purposes do not qualify. The recital gives two examples: systems for monitoring water pressure and fire alarm controlling systems in cloud computing centres.

REFERENCES

questions.question: Is the AI system intended to be used to determine access, admission, or to assign individuals to educational and vocational training institutions or programs?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS COVERED
This area covers AI used in or by schools, universities and training providers at any level, including vocational and adult education, in four specific ways: deciding who is admitted or which programme a person is placed in; evaluating learning results; assessing the level of education a person will receive or can access; and monitoring students for prohibited behaviour during tests.

What counts is a consequential judgement about the learner, such as a final or counting grade, a placement or an exam-integrity decision. Ongoing feedback and learning support, and tools that students choose to use on their own, are generally not covered unless they lead to a recognised qualification. Checking submitted homework for plagiarism is not test monitoring, and systems mainly aimed at training teachers fall outside this area.


REFERENCES

questions.question: Is the AI system intended to be used to place targeted job advertisements?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS COVERED
This area covers AI used to recruit or select people, including self-employed persons: placing job advertisements for a concrete vacancy, analysing and filtering applications, and evaluating candidates. It also covers AI used during the working relationship to decide on pay, working conditions, promotion or termination, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, and to monitor and evaluate performance or behaviour. Employees, freelancers and platform workers are included.

A system is covered even if a human formally takes the decision, as long as the AI output significantly influences it. Generally not covered: generic employer-branding advertisements, purely descriptive steps such as converting file formats, task allocation based only on neutral facts such as availability, and tools used purely for safety or legal compliance.

questions.question: Is the AI system intended to be used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS COVERED
(a) Systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits and services; (b) systems used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or to establish their credit score, with the exception of systems used for detecting financial fraud; (c) systems used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance; (d) systems used to evaluate and classify emergency calls, or to dispatch or prioritise emergency first response services (police, firefighters, medical aid), and emergency healthcare patient triage systems.

SCORING AND PROFILING
Credit scoring and insurance risk assessment may involve profiling within the meaning of the GDPR (evaluation of personal aspects such as economic situation or reliability). If a system profiles natural persons, it is always high-risk and the derogation in Art. 6(3) is unavailable. A social score that leads to unjustified or unfavourable treatment may fall under the prohibition in Art. 5(1)(c) (Prohibited Practices).

REFERENCES
T. Fülöp, P. Poindl, commentary on Art. 27; G. Couneson, commentary on Art. 6 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024

questions.question: Is the AI system intended to be used by competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a person's risk, including security, irregular migration or health risks?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS COVERED
This row is about AI used by or for competent public authorities, or EU agencies, in migration, asylum and border control. It covers four uses: lie-detector-type tools; assessing the security, irregular-migration or health risk posed by a person who wants to enter or has entered a Member State; helping to examine asylum, visa and residence applications and related complaints, including judging evidence; and detecting, recognising or identifying people, except checking travel documents.

What counts is the purpose the system is built for, not where it runs. A tool that gives an individual traveller a risk score or flag is covered; pure statistics that never point to individual people are not. A system used only for search and rescue is not border control, but a system that is also meant for border control is covered.

WHAT IS COVERED
Two types of AI system are covered here. The first is AI that a court or other judicial authority (or someone acting for it) uses to help research and interpret facts and the law, or to apply the law to a concrete case. The same applies to out-of-court dispute resolution bodies, such as arbitration, when the outcome has legal effects for the parties. questions.question: Is the AI system used for profiling of natural persons?
questions.ownerContext:
PROFILING
As a rule, a system used in one of the listed sensitive areas is high-risk. A provider can claim an exit only if the system does not pose a significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, in practice because it does not materially influence the outcome of a decision.

The question works in steps. First: does the system profile people, that is, automatically use personal data to evaluate personal aspects such as work performance, finances, health, interests, behaviour or location? If yes, there is no exit. Second, if not: according to the Commission's draft guidance there is no separate risk analysis; the test is whether at least one of four conditions is met. The system only performs a narrow procedural task; only improves a human activity that is already finished; only detects decision patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or only prepares an assessment. These conditions are read narrowly.

WHO IS AN AUTHORISED REPRESENTATIVE
An authorised representative is a person or company in the EU that a provider based outside the EU has formally chosen to act for it in the EU. Three things must all be true: you are located or established in the EU; the provider has given you a written mandate, meaning a written authorisation that sets out the tasks you act for it; and you have accepted that mandate.

The role exists for providers outside the EU of high-risk AI systems and of general-purpose AI models (models that can competently perform a wide range of different tasks). Simply selling, distributing or working with a non-EU provider's product does not make you its authorised representative. Without a written mandate that you accepted, you do not hold the role.

questions.question: Are you a natural or legal person who uses the AI system under your own responsibility?
questions.ownerContext:
WHO IS A DEPLOYER
You are a deployer if you use an AI system and you are the one who decides whether and how it is used. The test is authority, which means taking responsibility for the decision to use the system and for the way it is used, including what is done with its outputs. You do not need to operate the technology yourself, and you stay the deployer if contractors or freelancers use it on your behalf and under your control.

You are not a deployer if you only commission a result without deciding whether and how AI is used, or if you merely pass on or are exposed to AI-generated content. Employees acting on their employer's instructions are not separate deployers; their organisation is. A private person using AI purely for personal, non-professional reasons is not a deployer; any use linked to a job, business or regular income is professional.

questions.ownerContext:
WHO IS A PROVIDER
You are a provider if your organisation stands behind an AI system or a general-purpose AI model: you develop it, or have it developed for you, and place it on the market or start using it under your own name or trademark. questions.question: Is the AI system intended to interact with natural persons?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The question is whether your AI system is meant to deal directly with real people, for example as a chatbot, voice assistant or a robot that responds to people. Four things must come together: it is an AI system (not a simple rule-based auto-reply); it is meant to interact, meaning people give input and the system genuinely responds; the interaction is direct (not through a person who only passes on AI output); and the counterpart is a natural person, that is, a human being, not another machine.

Two exceptions change the answer. The first applies where it is obvious that one is dealing with an AI system, judged from the viewpoint of a reasonably well-informed, observant and careful person in that situation; this is read strictly. The second applies to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, unless the public can use them to report a crime.

questions.question: Does the AI system generate or manipulate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The question is whether your AI system creates or changes content that people can see, hear or read: audio, images, video or text, or a mix of these. "Generate" means the system produces new material, for instance an image or a song from a prompt. "Manipulate" means it alters existing material, such as a photo, a voice recording or a text. It is enough that AI is involved; mixing with human-made material does not take the content out of scope. General-purpose AI systems are included.

Not in scope are systems that only select, rank or arrange existing content, outputs that are source code or very short strings such as labels and captions, and machine-to-machine data that no person sees. Also excluded are systems that only help with standard editing (spelling, grammar, small colour corrections), systems that do not substantially change the input or its meaning, and systems authorised by law for criminal-law enforcement.

WHAT IS CAUSED BY THE AI SYSTEM
"Synthetic" means a content created by an AI system, including content that modifies a real photo or text supplied by the user; this is confirmed by the wording that outputs must be detectable as generated or manipulated. The goals of the rule are twofold: to tell what comes from a human and what from a machine, and to tell what comes from a reliable, genuine source and what was produced artificially. The marking does not have to take the same form as the content: artificial audio may, for example, be marked by text on the carrier, if the requirements are met.

questions.question: Does the AI system generate or manipulate audio or visual content, including images or video, that would falsely appear to be authentic or truthful (deepfake)?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The question is whether your AI system produces or alters images, audio or video in a way that makes a "deep fake". Three things must come together: the content is created or changed by AI; it resembles something that really exists or could plausibly exist, such as a real person, object, place, organisation or event; and it would falsely appear to someone to be authentic or true.

The last point is judged objectively, from the context and the audience you can reasonably foresee, including children or the elderly; you do not need any intention to deceive. High realism makes a deep fake more likely but is not decisive on its own. Obviously unreal content (humans flying, dragons) is not a deep fake, and AI-assisted touch-ups that barely affect how authentic the content looks, such as colour correction or noise reduction, usually are not either. Use authorised by law for criminal-law enforcement is exempt.

WHAT IS A DEEP FAKE
Art. 3(60) defines a deep fake as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful. The commentary on Art. 3(60) treats the three elements as cumulative. "Generated" means that the AI system creates entirely new material, for example an image of a person at an event they never attended, created from a text prompt; "manipulated" means that AI modifies existing material, for example a genuine recording of a politician's speech in which the spoken words are changed while the original facial expression and voice are kept. "Entity" means an institution. Not every AI-generated content is a deep fake: the content must have the potential to mislead an average recipient, who is the benchmark.

questions.question: Are you using an AI system that generates or manipulates text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The first part asks whether AI-generated or AI-changed text is published to inform the public about matters of public interest. Three elements: the text is published, meaning open to a large number of unrelated readers, even behind a paywall (private and internal company communications are not); it aims to communicate knowledge, opinions or facts; and it concerns matters relevant to society at large, locally to internationally, such as politics, public services, public health or consumer safety.

The second part asks whether the exception applies. It needs both: a real human review or editorial control (an actual check of substance by someone with the knowledge, including fact-checking; spell-checking or automated review is not enough), and a person or organisation holding editorial responsibility for the publication. AI changes made after sign-off cancel the exception. Use authorised by law for criminal-law enforcement is also exempt.

questions.question: Are you using an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE 
The question is whether you use an AI system that reads people's biometric data, such as face, voice or body movement, to work out their emotions or intentions, or to sort them into categories.

Emotion recognition covers feelings such as happiness, sadness, anger or excitement. It does not cover physical states such as pain or fatigue, nor the mere detection of readily apparent expressions, like a smile or a raised voice, unless used to infer an emotion.

Biometric categorisation means assigning people to groups, for example by sex, age, hair or eye colour, personality traits or ethnic origin. It is not about identifying a specific person. A feature that is purely ancillary to another commercial service and technically indispensable for it is not covered. Systems that the law permits for detecting, preventing or investigating crime are exempt.

questions.question: Does the AI system make decisions about individuals, or does it assist with such decisions?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The question is whether the high-risk AI system you use takes decisions about individual people, or supports a person who takes such decisions. It concerns systems that fall under one of the high-risk use areas listed in Annex III of the AI Act, for example in employment, education or access to essential services.

Only decisions that relate to natural persons, that is, human beings, count. Decisions about companies or other legal entities are not what this question is about. The question is about your use of the system, as a deployer, in decisions of this kind.
